explanation.hanzi: “几”用来问数量，一般用在估计答案小于十的时候，比如问家里几口人、小孩几岁。“几”后面要加量词：几口人、几岁。数目可能比较大时，一般不用“几”。
explanation.english: "几" asks "how many" when you expect a small answer — usually under ten: the number of people in a family, a child's age, the time of day. Like a number, 几 needs a measure word after it: 几口人, 几岁. When the answer could be large, Chinese speakers use a different question word, which you'll meet later. Just as with 谁 and 哪, don't add 吗 to a question with 几.

explanation.hanzi: 学会一到十，就能说一到九十九。十一到十九是“十＋个位”；整十是“几＋十”，比如二十、五十；其他的数是“几＋十＋个位”，比如三十五、九十九。数数和在数字最后时，“一”读一声。
explanation.english: Once you know 一 to 十, you can build every number up to 99 like Lego. 11–19 are "ten + unit": 十一 (11), 十五 (15). Round tens are "unit + ten": 二十 (20), 七十 (70). Everything else is "unit + ten + unit": 三十五 (35), 九十九 (99). Remember the tone change of 一 from Lesson 4: it stays yī when counting and at the end of a number (十一 shíyī, 二十一 èrshíyī).

examples.hanzi: 我朋友的女儿今年十一岁了。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ péngyou de nǚ'ér jīnnián shíyī suì le.
examples.english: My friend's daughter turned eleven this year.

explanation.hanzi: “了”放在句子最后，表示情况有了变化，出现了新的情况。“她七岁了”的意思是她以前不是七岁，现在到了七岁。说年龄时常用“……岁了”，问的时候也可以说“几岁了？”“多大了？”。
explanation.english: "了" at the very end of a sentence signals that something has changed — a new situation now holds that didn't before. 她七岁了 means "she's seven now" (she has reached that age). This is why ages are so often said with ……岁了, and asked with 几岁了？ or 多大了？. The same 了 works beyond age: 是学生了 — "is a student now".

examples.english: Wang Ming is a university student now.

explanation.hanzi: “多＋形容词”可以问程度，“多大”就是问年龄。问同龄人或者年轻人用“你多大？”或“你今年多大？”；问小孩子一般用“几岁”；问老人要用更客气的说法，比如“您多大年纪了？”。
explanation.english: 多 + adjective asks "how (much)…?", so 多大 — literally "how big" — asks someone's age. Choose the question to fit the person: for friends, classmates and other adults around your own age, say 你(今年)多大？; for young children, 几岁？ is more natural, since you expect a number under ten; for elderly people, a more respectful form is used (您多大年纪了？), which you'll learn later.

explanation.hanzi: “儿”加在别的音节后面时，不再单独成一个音节，而是让前面音节的韵母带上卷舌动作，拼音只加一个r，这叫“儿化”。北京话里儿化特别多。注意：“女儿”的“儿”是单独的音节ér，不是儿化。
explanation.english: When 儿 is added after another syllable it often stops being a syllable of its own: instead, you curl your tongue up at the end of the previous syllable, and pinyin just adds an r. This is called erhua, and it is especially common in Beijing speech. If the syllable ends in -n or -i, that sound drops out (wán + r → wánr, said "war"). Careful: in 女儿 nǚ'ér, 儿 is a full syllable meaning "child" — that is not erhua.

explanation.hanzi: 汉语有六对声母，只差在送不送气：b/p、d/t、g/k、j/q、z/c、zh/ch。送气音发音时有一股很强的气流，不送气音气流很弱。把一张纸放在嘴前练习：读p、t、k、q、c、ch时纸会动。
explanation.english: Six pairs of Chinese initials differ only in aspiration — a puff of air: b/p, d/t, g/k, j/q, z/c, zh/ch. The second of each pair is said with a strong burst of breath; the first has almost none, so Chinese b sounds a bit like the p in "spin", not the b in "bin". Hold a sheet of paper in front of your mouth: it should flutter on p, t, k, q, c, ch and stay still on b, d, g, j, z, zh. Getting this right changes meaning — bǎo "full" vs pǎo "run".

explanation.hanzi: a、o、e开头的音节放在别的音节后面时，如果音节界限可能混淆，要用隔音符号“'”隔开，比如nǚ'ér、Xī'ān。
explanation.english: When a syllable beginning with a, o or e follows another syllable in the same word, pinyin inserts an apostrophe to show where one syllable ends and the next begins. Without it, Xī'ān (Xi'an, two syllables) could be misread as xiān (one syllable). The mark is silent; it just tells you to start a new syllable.

singleComponentChars.etymology: A picture of a stream: the central line is the flowing current and the strokes on each side are drops and ripples. Squeezed onto the left of other characters it becomes the three-dot water radical 氵, as in 汉.
The oldest form shows a woman kneeling with her arms folded in front of her. It appears on the left of many characters about women and family, such as 好 and 她.

singleComponentChars.meaning: particle marking a change or completion; (liǎo) to finish
singleComponentChars.etymology: Early forms resemble a baby wrapped tightly so its arms don't show. The meaning "to end, to finish" developed from it, and today it is above all a grammar particle.
A grown person standing face-on with arms and legs stretched wide — as big as one can make oneself. Add a stroke on top and you get 天 "sky"; add a dot below and you get 太 "too, extremely".

Number chain: the group counts from 一 to 九十九 in turn; anyone who says a number with 七 in it must clap instead.

title.hanzi: 哥哥、弟弟、叔叔、阿姨：汉语的亲属称呼
title.english: Older, Younger, Father's Side, Mother's Side: Chinese Kinship Terms

culture.body:
English has one word for "brother" and one for "sister". Chinese doesn't: an older brother is 哥哥 (gēge), a younger brother 弟弟 (dìdi), an older sister 姐姐 (jiějie) and a younger sister 妹妹 (mèimei). Who was born first matters, because it traditionally decided responsibilities and respect within the family — so siblings usually call each other by these terms rather than by name.

The same precision applies to grandparents, aunts and uncles. Your father's parents are 爷爷 (yéye) and 奶奶 (nǎinai); your mother's parents are 外公 (wàigōng) and 外婆 (wàipó), or 姥爷 (lǎoye) and 姥姥 (lǎolao) in much of northern China. The 外 (wài, "outside") in those words is a trace of the old idea that a married daughter's family was "outside" the father's line. Your father's younger brother is 叔叔 (shūshu), while your mother's brother is 舅舅 (jiùjiu) — one English word, "uncle", covers half a dozen Chinese ones.

Family words also reach far beyond the family. A child is taught to greet any friendly adult man as 叔叔 and any woman as 阿姨 (āyí, "auntie"), and young people call a slightly older stranger 大哥 (dàgē) or 大姐 (dàjiě). So when 小美 calls Anna 安娜阿姨, she isn't saying they're related — she's being polite.
